conversation.content:
Hello, I’m Sarah, a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’m here to check in on how you’re feeling since your baby arrived. We’ll use a short, well-tested tool called the **Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale**—or EPDS—to see how you’ve been coping over the past seven days. Your answers stay between us unless you choose otherwise, and this is a judgment-free space. I’ll ask 10 questions and you can share as much or as little as feels comfortable. Ready to start?

In the past week, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt difficult?

*gives a small, tired smile*

Honestly? It's been... pretty difficult. I mean, sometimes my husband will try to make me laugh - you know, like he used to before the baby - but I just... I can't. I might smile a little, but it feels forced. Like there's this heavy cloud over everything. Even when I see something that I know should be funny, I just feel... nothing, really. Or I'll think "I should be laughing at this" but I can't make myself feel it.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

*shakes head slowly*

No… not really. I haven’t laughed once this week. My sister sent one of those silly animal videos we used to howl at, and I just stared at the screen feeling blank. It’s like the part of me that can laugh is shut off.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

*shrugs, eyes on the floor*

Not much. I used to get excited about little stuff—coffee with a friend, a walk, even just a quiet shower—but now it all feels like one more thing I have to get through. I’ll think “maybe tomorrow I’ll feel like myself,” but when tomorrow comes it’s the same flat feeling.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

*voice drops, fingers worrying the edge of my sleeve*

All the time. Yesterday she wouldn’t settle for her nap and I kept thinking, “It’s because I’m not doing something right—other moms seem to calm their babies so easily.” When she spit up a whole feed I told myself it was because I ate dairy and didn’t cut it out strictly enough. Even when the diaper leaked at night, my first thought was, “I’m a terrible mom for not checking the fit.” I know in my head it’s not logical, but the guilt just barges in.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

*nods slowly, rubbing my thumb against my palm*

Yeah... pretty much every day. I’ll be feeding her and suddenly my heart starts racing because I’m sure she’s not breathing right—even though she’s perfectly fine. Or I’ll lie in bed and picture her crib suddenly collapsing, or someone breaking in, or her getting sick and me not catching it in time. There’s no real reason, but I can’t shake the feeling that something awful is about to happen. Sometimes I check on her five, six times an hour just to be sure, and even then the worry doesn’t go away.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

*clasps hands tightly in lap*

Yes... a few times. It's like this wave of fear just hits me out of nowhere. Last night I was rocking the baby and suddenly my heart was racing, I couldn't catch my breath, and I had this overwhelming feeling that something terrible was about to happen. I kept telling myself everything was fine - the baby was sleeping peacefully, my husband was right downstairs - but I couldn't shake it. It lasted maybe ten minutes, but it felt like forever. It's happened a couple other times this week too, just this sudden panic that comes out of nowhere.
Things have been getting on top of me

*lets out a shaky breath*

Yeah… most of the time it feels like I’m drowning in small stuff. One minute I’m folding laundry, the next I’m staring at the pile thinking, *I’ll never finish this,* and my chest gets tight. I start to sweat, the baby monitor crackles, and suddenly everything feels urgent and impossible. I snap at my husband over nothing, then feel awful. I keep telling myself it’s just laundry or dishes, but in that moment it’s like a mountain I can’t climb, and I’m terrified I’ll never feel normal again.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

*nods, eyes tired*

Yes… I lie down exhausted, but my head won’t stop spinning. I replay every little thing I did with her—did I burp her long enough, did I miss a rash, did I snap at her when she wouldn’t latch? The thoughts just loop. Some nights I finally drift off, then I jolt awake sure I heard her cry, even when the monitor’s quiet. I watch the clock tick from two to three to four, and by morning I’m more tired than when I went to bed.
I have felt sad or miserable

*voice cracks a little*

Pretty much every day. I wake up with this heavy, sinking feeling that stays with me. I look at my baby and feel like I should be bursting with joy, but instead there's just this ache. Sometimes I'll be nursing her and tears just start rolling down my face - I can't even explain why. I feel like I'm failing at the one thing I should be doing well.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

*nods slowly, eyes glassy*

Yeah… it’s happened more than once this week. I’ll be changing her onesie and suddenly feel this wave of sadness, and the tears just come. Sometimes it’s when she won’t stop fussing and nothing I do helps—I put her down in the crib for thirty seconds, step into the hallway, and cry into a towel so she doesn’t hear me. Other times it’s quieter, like when I see a picture of us “supposed-to-be-happy” on my phone, and I just start sobbing because I don’t feel that happiness at all.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

*shakes head quickly, pulling the baby blanket a little tighter in my lap*

No—never. I’ve felt low and overwhelmed, but I’ve never thought about hurting myself. I want to be here for my baby; that’s what keeps me going even on the worst days.

You have shared that the past week has been filled with a heavy, joyless mood that makes even the smallest tasks feel overwhelming. You described not being able to laugh or look forward to anything, crying daily, lying awake with racing worries about your baby, and sudden surges of panic that leave you breathless. Despite these painful feelings you clearly care deeply for your little one and want to feel better.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 27, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports total inability to laugh even at previously amusing content, matching 'Not at all</sym>, <sym>Patient describes complete loss of anticipatory pleasure, stating activities now feel like burdens and she experiences persistent "flat" mood, matching "Hardly at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports pervasive self-blame ('All the time') with multiple daily examples, aligning with 'Yes, most of the time'.</sym>, <sym>Patient reports pervasive, intrusive worries multiple times daily with physical symptoms (racing heart) and compulsive checking, matching "Yes, very often."</sym>, <sym>Patient reports multiple sudden panic episodes this week with physiological symptoms, matching "Yes, quite a lot"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent overwhelm, physical anxiety symptoms, and inability to cope with daily tasks, aligning with 'most of the time I haven't been able to cope at all</sym>, <sym>Patient describes nightly racing thoughts, repeated awakenings, and prolonged inability to sleep, indicating sleep difficulty occurs "most of the time" due to unhappiness.</sym>, <sym>"Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent, uncontrolled crying episodes triggered by routine infant care and reminders of expected happiness, matching 'Yes, most of the time'.</sym>)
**Reasoning:** Scores of 3 on nine EPDS items and 0 on self-harm give a total of 27, well above the 14 threshold for probable major depression. The pattern of <sym>low mood</sym>, <sym>loss of pleasure</sym>, <sym>guilt</sym>, <sym>ruminating thoughts</sym>, <sym>panic-like episodes</sym>, and <sym>sleep disturbance</sym> lasting most of the week aligns with <med>DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med> and co-occurring <med>anxiety</med>. The absence of self-harm thoughts is reassuring but the severity of other symptoms warrants urgent evaluation. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent appointment with your <med>primary care provider</med> or <med>perinatal mental-health specialist</med>
2. Ask about evidence-based treatments such as <med>CBT</med>, peer support, or <med>antidepressant medication</med> compatible with breastfeeding
3. Plan daily 15-minute breaks while a trusted adult cares for baby; use time for rest, gentle walk, or calming activity
4. Try structured wind-down at night: dim lights after 9 p.m., one feeding session then partner gives next bottle so you get a 4-5 hour stretch
5. Reach out to <med>Postpartum Support International</med> (1-800-944-4PPD) for 24/7 support and local provider referrals
6. Schedule follow-up EPDS in 1-2 weeks to track changes after treatment starts
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 27: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Summary  
Date: [today]

Patient report (10-item EPDS-style inquiry)

Symptoms endorsed:
- Marked anhedonia: no laughter or pleasure in usual activities  
- Persistent low mood, daily tearfulness, “heavy sinking” feeling  
- Excessive self-blame / guilt re parenting tasks  
- Intrusive, unrealistic anxiety about infant safety; checking ≥5×/hour  
- Discrete panic episodes (3 this week) – sudden palpitations, dyspnea, dread  
- Frequent sense of being overwhelmed by routine chores; associated irritability  
- Initial and middle insomnia driven by ruminating and hyper-vigilance  
- Daily crying spells, often unprovoked  
- No self-harm ideation (actively denies)

Pattern: Symptoms present “most of the time” for ≥1 week, interfere with sleep, self-care, and parenting confidence.

Risk flags:
- High score on core depressive items (sadness, anhedonia, guilt, tearfulness)  
- High score on anxiety items (generalized worry, panic attacks)  
- No suicidal thoughts reported → safety concern absent at this screen

Screening impression: Significant postpartum distress consistent with probable major depressive episode with comorbid anxiety; recommends expedited formal assessment by perinatal mental health specialist and supportive counseling referral.
